title: Weekend Wine Down| Leaning Into Liens
content: I'm Sarah Shark and this is my weekly line down where I open a bottle of wine and talk about the themes of the week. This week is sunny with a chance of flowers. It's going to charm me a little title and it's delicious. I've had it before. It's carbonated. I love bubbles. I worked at a workbench tribunal once. It was an investigator there who was quite scary and he used to say, I only drink the pink stuff because he only loved pink bubbles. And so when every sparkling rosé it always reminds me of him. It didn't get wine glass. A few moments later. So I'm no longer at a workbench tribunal. I help people with mergers and acquisitions when they buy and sell different businesses. This week I had a theme that came out a lot which was Lanes. This is where I'm most lame against something. Lanes like L.I.E. in against the assets of a company and it's funny how it comes up twice in a week. Hold on. It's really good. 9% alcohol per volume. I don't know if that's higher or not, but it's the end of the week. In one instance I had the buyer and then the other one is a seller and they both were surprised by the effect of having a lean against the assets of the company. That's a really big deal and when I talk to my clients I like to call it out as early as possible because if you don't it can completely destroy your deal when you get on the road and you waste a much time and expense and the only people who have one are the lawyers. I don't really like to do things for no reason even if it means I'm getting paid so I would rather have a deal diet really than a diet like so in both cases I'll give you the example of one. In one the buyer was trying to buy a company he knew that there had been an EIDL loan in the past. An EID loan is an economic injury disaster loan that can provide up to $2 million from financial assistance to small businesses or private non-profit organizations that suffer substantial economic injury as a result of the declared disaster regardless of whether the applicants sustained physical damage. So when that happens I always say is there a lean because the SBA did all this economic injury disaster loan? Is that what another search come up with that on there? I felt pretty good about that acronym. But there's like COVID relief type loans. They came out with them for everybody but in almost every case they filed a lien which you can go on and do like a UCC lien search and find a lien against the assets of the company and the way they describe the assets that are lien is so all included. It actually includes the word all tangible and intangible personal properties. So if you are a company and you have one of those the government filed a lien almost surely and it probably included not just the personal property that you can touch but also the personal property you can't touch which is everything. I can't think of anything that wouldn't fit into those boxes really. And if there was an EID loan at any point there is likely a lien out there. They do not automatically remove the lien. You want to check in on that. The problem is I've had deals killed because they don't know that there's still a lien out there for whatever reason. Maybe the partner took out the loan and then disappeared and nobody really knew it was out there. Or sometimes the SBA doesn't automatically remove the lien and if you don't have enough lead time to get them to do that or request a lien release and if the buyer won't accept or the bank won't accept and just the letter saying it was paid off then you can be in a big scruffful at the end of closing. So why doesn't matter? Because it'll kill your deal. It's the biggest one. It's an ownership issue. So if somebody files a lien they're saying and that you as the seller don't fully own those assets and that means you can't sell them to someone. You can't sell somebody something you don't own. Some buyers have a risk tolerance that's high enough that they would even take a lien asset and maybe it depends on what it is. But let's say it's clientless and you know that the bank has a superior right to go get those. You pay the same amount for something that essentially is first owned by someone else. So nine times out of a 10 maybe 99 times out of 100. The buyer is going to want you to pay off all of the loans out there that have resulted in all lien. Other things that surprise people are like we're evolving lines of credit. You know you get overwhelmed I think by all the loan package documents you don't read them all. And you don't realize they're also going and filing this very publicly findable lien against your assets. So if that happens it could kill your deal. It will almost certainly delay it unless you call it out at the very beginning and start working on ways to sell for it. The thing that I had this week was in both cases unfortunately the purchase amount wasn't greater than the debt amount. So you know saying hey if you have a $500,000 business I'm going to pay you $500,000 for it but you have a $700,000 loan. You know that's not going to result in anyone taking that lien off of the assets and so you're not going to pay it off at closing even though that might be a good deal for you because you're running a business that you don't want to be running anymore and you just want to get out and start cutting your losses you can't make that happen very easily. So that is one of the issues that I had both sides. A seller trying to sell who said I get that I'm in debt I get that I have this lien. I'll keep my business open I'll keep paying this loan that has resulted in the lien I'll keep paying it off but the buyer said hey listen I'm not going to buy assets that are clouded title because it doesn't make any sense for me. In the other case I had a buyer who really wanted to buy assets. She said I wouldn't buy these assets I don't care that there's a lien. I mean what is the SBA what is the government going to do come take this client list that doesn't make sense they don't know what to do with it. I feel dead about it personally but they were going to finance the deal and then bank said no way to help because of that you know her dreams were crushed and the seller couldn't get out either so lien's big deal big threshold issue you don't want to wait too long to dig in on that and another thing that I think is worth thinking about is hold on. Really good is that the banks usually don't want to run a lien search until pretty close to closing and a really thorough one can cost some money. In Colorado where I lived you can look it up for free but that's not always the case. It's worth considering doing that on the early side instead of waiting for the bank to do it like 72 hours before closing if there's a bank because when you're surprised by that boy it's a scramble and everyone's so displeased and I don't want that for anyone so look at millions of Lehman to Lehman removal maybe this is my weekly windout thanks for tuning in if you get a P.A. value please like and subscribe.
description:
Sarah Sharp's weekly wine down is here 🍷

This week, she's venturing into Liens while sipping on sparkling rosé.

But it's not all about the wine.🍷

Sarah highlights something critical with deals: understanding liens.

Liens can derail deals if not addressed early.

She shares stories where buyers and sellers were caught off guard by existing liens.

-----
Your Host:

Sara Sharp - Deal Attorney
LinkedIn: 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/sara-sharp-9a2a98b/
Websites:
www.dealacademy.org
www.skandslegal.com
